questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine four subfields using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A departmental overview lists four approaches: one studies living cultures, one studies human biology and fossils, one studies material remains, and one studies language in use. Each claims a distinct kind of evidence but a shared object, humanity.

questions.stem: Which statement about four subfields is best supported by the account?

options.text: Anthropology is organized into cultural, biological, archaeological, and linguistic subfields that together study humanity in all its dimensions.
Anthropology is a single undivided discipline that studies only the biology of past human populations and their fossil record.
options.misconception: The four subfields depend on one another and each contributes a different kind of evidence about the same human condition.

options.text: The four subfields are sociology, psychology, economics, and political science working together under a single umbrella.
options.misconception: It mistakes a shared object of study for a single method, ignoring that each subfield has its own evidence and training.

options.text: Anthropology is divided into ancient history, modern history, archaeology, and the study of classical languages.
options.misconception: It borrows the fourfold division from the social sciences and mislabels sociology and economics as anthropological subfields.

questions.explanation: It restricts anthropology to the remote past, leaving out living cultures and the linguistic study of present-day communities.
questions.hint: A truly anthropological answer joins evidence about bodies, artifacts, language, and custom rather than isolating one kind.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine holism using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A research team studying a highland community records crop yields, kinship rules, ritual calendars, and soil chemistry in the same field season, insisting that none of these can be understood in isolation from the others.

questions.stem: The evidence most strongly supports which claim about holism?

options.text: Holism means that a researcher should collect as many unrelated facts as possible without asking how they connect to one another.
options.misconception: The team treats ecology, kinship, and ritual as interdependent parts of one social formation rather than separate topics.

options.text: Holism is the commitment to understand any part of human life in the context of the whole system of which it is a part.
Holism is the belief that biological factors always determine cultural practices and that social life can be reduced to genes.
options.misconception: It confuses holism with mere breadth of data collection, missing the claim that the parts are systematically related.

options.text: Holism requires that anthropologists study only small, isolated societies that have had no contact with the wider world.
options.misconception: It turns holism into biological determinism, a position most anthropologists explicitly reject.

questions.explanation: It mistakes holism for a ban on studying complex or connected societies, which is not part of the idea.
questions.hint: The value of the holistic approach is that a change in one domain can be traced through consequences in others.

options.misconception: The project brings together lived practice, material remains, bodies, and speech to test a common account.

options.text: Integrating subfields requires abandoning archaeology because it is the least scientific of the approaches.
options.misconception: It mistakes integration for separation, missing the point that the findings are combined.

options.text: Integrating subfields means that linguistic data must always be treated as less reliable than genetic data.
options.misconception: It demotes a whole subfield on false grounds rather than weighing different evidence fairly.

options.text: Integrating subfields allows researchers to check one kind of evidence against another and build a fuller account.

questions.explanation: It imposes an arbitrary hierarchy of evidence that anthropology does not support.
questions.hint: The strength of integration is that a claim supported by several independent kinds of evidence is stronger.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine four subfields using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A departmental overview lists four approaches: one studies living cultures, one studies human biology and fossils, one studies material remains, and one studies language in use. Each claims a distinct kind of evidence but a shared object, humanity.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about four subfields follows from the observation?

options.text: Anthropology is organized into cultural, biological, archaeological, and linguistic subfields that together study humanity in all its dimensions.
Anthropology is a single undivided discipline that studies only the biology of past human populations and their fossil record.
options.misconception: The four subfields depend on one another and each contributes a different kind of evidence about the same human condition.

options.text: The four subfields are sociology, psychology, economics, and political science working together under a single umbrella.
options.misconception: It mistakes a shared object of study for a single method, ignoring that each subfield has its own evidence and training.

options.text: Anthropology is divided into ancient history, modern history, archaeology, and the study of classical languages.
options.misconception: It borrows the fourfold division from the social sciences and mislabels sociology and economics as anthropological subfields.

questions.explanation: It restricts anthropology to the remote past, leaving out living cultures and the linguistic study of present-day communities.
questions.hint: A truly anthropological answer joins evidence about bodies, artifacts, language, and custom rather than isolating one kind.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine holism using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A research team studying a highland community records crop yields, kinship rules, ritual calendars, and soil chemistry in the same field season, insisting that none of these can be understood in isolation from the others.

questions.stem: How should holism be understood in this context?

options.text: Holism means that a researcher should collect as many unrelated facts as possible without asking how they connect to one another.
options.misconception: The team treats ecology, kinship, and ritual as interdependent parts of one social formation rather than separate topics.

options.text: Holism is the commitment to understand any part of human life in the context of the whole system of which it is a part.
Holism is the belief that biological factors always determine cultural practices and that social life can be reduced to genes.
options.misconception: It confuses holism with mere breadth of data collection, missing the claim that the parts are systematically related.

options.text: Holism requires that anthropologists study only small, isolated societies that have had no contact with the wider world.
options.misconception: It turns holism into biological determinism, a position most anthropologists explicitly reject.

questions.explanation: It mistakes holism for a ban on studying complex or connected societies, which is not part of the idea.
questions.hint: The value of the holistic approach is that a change in one domain can be traced through consequences in others.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine cultural anthropology using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A scholar spends a year in a riverine town, attending markets and weddings and conducting long interviews about how residents understand fairness and obligation.

questions.stem: What is the best reading of cultural anthropology here?

options.text: Cultural anthropology is the study of stone tools and settlement patterns reconstructed from excavated sites.
options.misconception: The scholar is documenting the shared meanings and practices that organize everyday life in a contemporary community.

options.text: Cultural anthropology is the study of the human genome and the biological variation among living populations.
options.misconception: It assigns the researcher the work of an archaeologist, who studies material remains rather than living people.

options.text: Cultural anthropology is the study of learned patterns of thought and behavior in living human communities.
Cultural anthropology is the branch that describes the grammar and sound systems of undocumented languages.
options.misconception: It assigns the researcher the work of a biological anthropologist, who studies bodies and genes rather than meanings.

questions.explanation: It assigns the researcher the work of a linguist, whose focus is linguistic structure rather than social life as a whole.
questions.hint: Long-term engagement and attention to local categories are hallmarks of this subfield's approach.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: examine biological anthropology using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A researcher measures skeletal remains from a coastal cemetery and compares tooth wear and isotope ratios with records of diet from the same site.

questions.stem: Which account of biological anthropology is most consistent with the facts?

options.text: Biological anthropology studies the grammatical rules of a language as spoken by a single community.
options.misconception: The researcher is using bodily remains to infer diet and health, a core concern of the biological subfield.

options.text: Biological anthropology studies the rituals and deities of a living religious community.
options.misconception: It assigns the work to linguistic anthropology, which does not analyze bone or isotope chemistry.

options.text: Biological anthropology studies the excavation and dating of pottery sequences at an archaeological site.
options.misconception: It assigns the work to cultural anthropology, whose usual evidence is not skeletal tissue.

options.text: Biological anthropology studies human biology, evolution, and variation, including the analysis of skeletal and fossil evidence.

questions.explanation: It assigns the work to archaeology, which may use such data but whose defining object is material culture and sites.
questions.hint: Isotopes and tooth wear are biological indicators that connect individual bodies to population-level patterns.
